Elements in Our World

What is everything made of? Today: atoms, elements, molecules, compounds and mixtures, how the periodic table works, where elements are found, what air is made of, metals and non-metals, and chemical reactions. There is a graph in most parts.

PART 1 Atoms and elements

LEARN
Everything around you is made of tiny particles called atoms. An atom is far too small to see, even with a microscope.
An element is a substance made of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into anything simpler. There are about 118 elements. Everything in the universe is made from them.
All three are elements: each box has only one type of atom (one colour).
LEARN · Chemical symbols
Every element has a symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital. A second letter is always small.
O = oxygen  ·  C = carbon  ·  Cl = chlorine  ·  Ca = calcium  ·  Mg = magnesium
Some symbols come from old Latin names:
ElementSymbolLatin nameElementSymbolLatin name
sodiumNanatriumcopperCucuprum
ironFeferrumgoldAuaurum
potassiumKkaliumsilverAgargentum
Capitals matter! Co is cobalt, an element. CO is carbon monoxide, a compound of carbon and oxygen.

PART 1 Molecules, compounds and mixtures

Molecule

Two or more atoms chemically joined (bonded) together. The atoms can be the same (O2) or different (H2O).

Compound

Two or more different elements chemically joined. It has new properties and is hard to separate.

Mixture

Two or more substances mixed but not joined. Each keeps its own properties. It is usually easy to separate.
LEARN · Reading a formula
A formula tells you which atoms are in a molecule and how many. The small number counts the atom just before it. No number means one.
FormulaAtoms in one moleculeTotal atomsElement or compound?
H2O (water)2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen3compound
CO2 (carbon dioxide)1 carbon + 2 oxygen3compound
O2 (oxygen gas)2 oxygen2element
Exam trap: O2 is a molecule, but it is not a compound. Count the types of atom, not the number of atoms. One type = element. Two or more types joined = compound.

Compound: new properties

Sodium is a soft metal that fizzes in water. Chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Joined together they make sodium chloride, the salt on your food.

Mixture: easy to separate

Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder: a magnet pulls the iron out. After heating they react to make iron sulfide, a compound, and the magnet no longer works.

PART 2 The periodic table

LEARN
The periodic table lists all the elements in order of their atomic number (the small number in each box).
The rows going across are called periods. The columns going down are called groups. Elements in the same group have similar properties: they react in a similar way.
THE FIRST 20 ELEMENTS
metal    non-metal
the staircase line between metals and non-metals
the whole table: 118 elements
(the dark outlines are the 20 above)
  • Metals are on the left and in the middle. Most elements are metals.
  • Non-metals are on the right of the staircase line. Hydrogen is a non-metal even though it sits on the left.
  • Group 1: very reactive soft metals. They fizz in water.
  • Group 7: reactive non-metals, such as chlorine.
  • Group 0: very unreactive gases, such as helium, neon and argon.

PART 3 Elements in the Earth

LEARN
The Earth's crust (the rocky outer layer) is made mostly of just eight elements. Most of these elements are not found on their own. They are joined to other elements in compounds. For example, sand is a compound of silicon and oxygen.

PART 4 The air we breathe

LEARN
Air is a mixture of gases. The gases are mixed together but not chemically joined, so each gas keeps its own properties. Some of the gases in air are elements and some are compounds.
GRAPH B · What is air made of? (percentage by volume)
GasFormulaIn the picture
nitrogenN2two blue atoms joined
oxygenO2two red atoms joined
argonArone grey atom on its own
carbon dioxideCO2one black + two red atoms joined
Why a pie chart? A pie chart shows how a whole (all of the air, 100%) is split into parts.

PART 5 Metals and non-metals

LEARN
Most elements are metals. They are on the left of the periodic table. Non-metals are on the right. We can sort elements by their properties: what they are like and how they behave.
PropertyMetalsNon-metals
Lookshinyusually dull
Conduct electricity?yes, good conductorsno, insulators
Conduct heat?yesno (poor)
Hit with a hammerbend into shape (malleable)solids break (brittle)
Sound when hitring (sonorous)dull thud
Melting pointusually highusually low
State at room temperaturesolid (except mercury)many are gases
Magnetic?only iron, nickel and cobaltno
Two famous exceptions: mercury is a metal but it is a liquid at room temperature. Graphite (a type of carbon) is a non-metal but it conducts electricity.
Careful: not all metals are magnetic. A magnet will not pick up aluminium or copper.

PART 6 Chemical reactions

LEARN
In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged and join in new ways to make a new substance. In a physical change (like melting or dissolving) no new substance is made, and it is usually easy to reverse.

Signs of a chemical reaction

  • a new substance is made
  • colour change
  • fizzing (a gas is made)
  • heat or light is given out
  • hard to reverse

Word equations

The substances we start with are the reactants. The new substances are the products.

reactants → products
magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide

Burning magnesium

Magnesium burns with a very bright white light. The magnesium atoms join with oxygen atoms from the air to make magnesium oxide, a white powder.

+
→
Naming tip: a compound of a metal and oxygen ends in -ide: magnesium oxide, copper oxide, iron oxide.
